islands.title: AI literacy
islands.learn: What AI, machine learning and large language models are, what they can and can't do yet, and the words you'll see everywhere: model, training, parameters, tokens, prompts.
islands.build: Use three AI tools on one real task from your work and write down where each one got it wrong.
know: The difference between AI, machine learning, deep learning and a large language model
What training means: a model adjusts its parameters to fit examples instead of following rules someone wrote
Why an LLM can sound sure and still be wrong: it predicts likely next tokens and doesn't look facts up
What a token, a parameter and a dataset are, in one sentence each
res: No coding, light math; about 6 weeks
Short course with a free certificate
10 videos, about 3.5 hours, includes how LLMs work
Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI

islands.title: Python
islands.learn: Variables, loops, functions, files and packages, then NumPy and pandas basics in a Jupyter or Google Colab notebook. Enough to read someone else's code and change it.
islands.build: A script that pulls data from a CSV file or a public API and prints a clean summary.
know: What variables, lists, dictionaries, loops and functions do, and when to use each
How to read a traceback and find the line that broke
How to install and import a package, and what a virtual environment is for
How a NumPy array differs from a Python list, and how to load a CSV into a pandas DataFrame
islands.note: CS50P's lectures were recorded in 2022, and its current term closes on 30 June 2027. It doesn't cover NumPy, pandas or notebooks, so work through the official NumPy and pandas guides in Google Colab or Jupyter before the math island.
res: CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python (CS50P)
10 weeks at 3 to 9 hours a week
100 Days of Code: The Complete Python Pro Bootcamp
About 57 hours of video, updated October 2026
NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners
Short official intro for new users
Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition

islands.title: Math for machine learning
islands.learn: Vectors and matrices, derivatives and gradients, probability and statistics. Every model you'll train rests on these three.
islands.build: Fit a straight line to some data with gradient descent you write yourself in NumPy, without an ML library.
know: What vectors and matrices are, and what multiplying a matrix by a vector does
What a derivative and a gradient tell you, and why gradient descent steps against the gradient
What a probability distribution, a mean and a variance describe
Why a model's loss is a function you can minimize, and where the chain rule comes in
res: Mathematics for Machine Learning and Data Science

islands.title: Machine learning basics
islands.learn: Supervised and unsupervised learning, train, validation and test splits, overfitting, and the classic models (linear and logistic regression, decision trees, gradient boosting) in scikit-learn.
islands.build: One project on a public dataset from start to finish: clean it, train two models and compare them on data they haven't seen.
know: Why you split data into training, validation and test sets, and what goes wrong if you don't
Overfitting and underfitting, and how to spot each from training and validation scores
Classification versus regression, and which metrics fit each (accuracy, precision and recall, error)
How linear regression, logistic regression and a decision tree each make a prediction
islands.note: Andrew Ng's course uses TensorFlow. Most of what comes after this island uses PyTorch, so expect to switch.
res: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Python
James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani and Taylor
Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch

islands.title: Deep learning
islands.learn: Neural networks, backpropagation, convolutional nets and transformers at a working level, all in PyTorch, and what actually happens on a GPU during training.
islands.build: Train an image classifier on your own photos and put it online as a small demo.
know: How a neural network turns inputs into an output, layer by layer
What backpropagation computes and how an optimizer uses it to update the weights
What one step of a training loop does: forward pass, loss, backward pass, update
Why convolutions suit images and attention suits sequences
What batch size and learning rate change, and why GPUs make training fast
res: Daniel Bourke and Andrei Neagoie on Udemy
About 52 hours; same material free at learnpytorch.io
The Little Book of Deep Learning
Christopher M. Bishop and Hugh Bishop

islands.title: LLM APIs and prompting
islands.learn: How an LLM produces text, then how to call one from code: system prompts, examples in the prompt, structured JSON output, and tokens and what they cost.
islands.build: A small tool that turns messy meeting notes into a clean follow-up email.
know: How an LLM generates text one token at a time, and what temperature changes
What the system prompt, the user messages and examples in the prompt each do
How to get structured output such as JSON and check it in your code
How tokens drive cost and context limits, and how to estimate what a request costs
islands.note: Skip old tutorials built on OpenAI's Assistants API. OpenAI shut it down in August 2026.
res: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
AI Engineer Core Track: LLM Engineering, RAG, QLoRA, Agents

islands.title: RAG: answers from your documents
islands.learn: Embeddings, vector search, chunking and retrieval-augmented generation, so a model answers from your own documents and cites them.
islands.build: A chatbot that answers questions from a folder of PDFs and shows the page each answer came from.
know: What an embedding is and why texts with similar meanings land close together
How vector search finds the right chunks, and how chunk size changes the answers
The whole RAG flow: chunk, embed, retrieve, add to the prompt, answer with citations
How to tell whether a bad answer came from retrieval or from generation
res: 10 weeks; no GPU, about $1 to $5 in API credits

islands.title: Agents and tools
islands.learn: Tool use (function calling), agent loops, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), memory, and how to tell when a fixed workflow will do the job better than an agent.
islands.build: An agent that researches a company on the web and drafts a one-page brief into a doc or sheet.
know: How tool use works: the model asks for a tool, your code runs it, the result goes back
What an agent loop is, and why it needs limits on steps, cost and permissions
What MCP standardizes and when you'd use it
When a fixed workflow is the better choice than an agent
res: About 3 to 4 hours per unit, free certificate
AI Engineer Agentic Track: The Complete Agent & MCP Course
Self-paced, uses Gemini and Google's ADK

islands.title: Evals and shipping
islands.learn: Test sets built from real examples, error analysis, LLM judges you've checked against people, then cost, latency, guardrails and monitoring once the app is live.
islands.build: Write 50 test cases from real use of one of your apps, fix the worst failure, and ship the better version.
know: How to build a test set from real examples and score outputs against it
How error analysis works: read the outputs, group the failures, fix the biggest group first
When you can trust an LLM judge, and how to check it against human labels
Which cost, latency and safety checks to set up before real users arrive
res: AI Evals for Engineers and PMs
Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, Maven

islands.title: Open models and Hugging Face
islands.learn: How transformers and tokenizers work inside, the Hugging Face libraries (Transformers, Datasets, the Hub), and running open-weight models on your own machine.
islands.build: Run an open-weight model locally and compare it with an API model on 20 of your own prompts.
know: How a tokenizer turns text into IDs, and why models split words differently
What happens inside a transformer block: attention, the feed-forward layer and residual connections
How to load an open-weight model with Transformers and run it on your own machine
How model size, precision (16-bit or 4-bit) and context length decide the memory you need

islands.title: Fine-tuning with LoRA
islands.learn: When fine-tuning beats prompting or RAG, how to build a training set, and supervised fine-tuning with LoRA and QLoRA on a single GPU.
islands.build: Fine-tune a small open model on about 1,000 examples of one task and measure it against the base model.
know: When fine-tuning is worth it compared with better prompts or RAG
How LoRA trains small adapter matrices instead of all the weights, and what QLoRA adds
How to build and clean a training set in the chat format the model expects
How to read training and validation loss to tell whether a run is working
islands.note: With 4-bit QLoRA, a 7B or 8B model fits in about 5 to 6 GB of GPU memory, by Unsloth's own figures. Google Colab's free tier offers limited GPU time to start.
res: LoRA and QLoRA on one GPU or Colab

islands.title: Preference tuning: RLHF, DPO and GRPO
islands.learn: How chat models learn to behave: instruction tuning, reward models, RLHF, DPO, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO) for reasoning.
islands.build: Use DPO to change one behavior of your fine-tuned model, then check that nothing else broke.
know: How a base model becomes a chat model: instruction tuning, then preference tuning
What a reward model learns, and how RLHF uses it
How DPO learns from pairs of better and worse answers without a separate reward model
What GRPO with verifiable rewards does for reasoning, and why it needs answers you can check
res: LLM Course, chapter 12: Build reasoning models
About 2 hours; labs run on Predibase

islands.title: Evaluate, quantize and serve
islands.learn: Public benchmarks versus your own task evals, quantization, and serving a model with tools such as vLLM, llama.cpp or Ollama, plus what each choice costs in speed and money.
islands.build: Quantize your model, serve it behind an API, and run your test set against it.
know: Why public benchmark scores may not predict how a model does on your task
What quantization trades: memory and speed against some accuracy
How vLLM, llama.cpp and Ollama differ, and which fits your hardware
How to compare your fine-tuned model with its base model on the same tests

islands.title: Neural nets from scratch
islands.learn: Write backpropagation yourself, then a character-level language model, until you understand every line a framework normally hides.
islands.build: Rebuild micrograd and makemore without looking at the reference code.
know: How backpropagation applies the chain rule through a graph of operations, step by step
Why gradients are reset each step, and what a learning rate that's too high or too low does
How a character-level model is trained to predict the next character
What PyTorch does for you, now that you've done it by hand

islands.title: A GPT from scratch
islands.learn: Attention, transformer blocks, the training loop and sampling. Write a GPT in PyTorch and load real GPT-2 weights into it.
islands.build: Train a small GPT on a text collection you care about and generate samples from it.
know: How self-attention lets each token look at earlier tokens, and why the mask hides the future
What queries, keys and values are, and why there are several attention heads
How a GPT is trained to predict the next token, and how sampling generates text
Why residual connections and layer norm keep deep networks trainable
res: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out
Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)

islands.title: Tokenizers, data and pretraining
islands.learn: Byte-pair tokenizers, cleaning web-scale data, pretraining, mixed precision, multi-GPU training and scaling laws.
islands.build: Run nanochat end to end: tokenizer, pretraining, fine-tuning and a chat interface for your own small model.
know: How byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary from raw text
Why filtering and deduplicating data matter as much as the model
What mixed precision and multi-GPU training speed up, and what they cost
What scaling laws say about model size, data and compute
islands.note: Expect to rent cloud GPUs here. nanochat's README puts a GPT-2-level run at about $48 on one 8-GPU node.
res: Stanford, Percy Liang and Tatsunori Hashimoto
Spring 2026 run: 19 lectures, 5 heavy coding assignments
A full ChatGPT-style training pipeline in one repo

islands.title: Scale and research
islands.learn: How large models train across many GPUs (data, tensor and pipeline parallelism), how reasoning models are trained with RL, and how to read and reproduce papers.
islands.build: Reproduce one result from a recent paper and publish your code and notes.
know: How data, tensor and pipeline parallelism split the work across GPUs
How reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning on checkable answers
How to read a paper: find the claim, the method and the experiment that tests it
How to reproduce a result and judge whether your numbers really match

islands.title: Vision foundations
islands.learn: Convolutional networks and vision transformers, transfer learning, and data augmentation for images.
islands.build: Fine-tune a pretrained image model to sort photos into categories you choose.
know: How a convolution detects patterns, and why stacked layers find bigger features
How a vision transformer turns an image into patches it treats like tokens
How transfer learning reuses a pretrained model for your own images
What data augmentation does, and when it can hurt
res: CS231n: Deep Learning for Computer Vision

islands.title: Detection, segmentation and multimodal
islands.learn: Object detection, segmentation, self-supervised learning, and models that connect images with text, such as CLIP and vision-language models.
islands.build: An app that finds and counts objects in photos or video and draws boxes around them.
know: The difference between classification, detection and segmentation outputs
How detection is scored with IoU and mean average precision
How CLIP learns a shared space for images and text
How a vision-language model answers questions about an image
res: Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2nd edition

islands.title: Language foundations
islands.learn: How text becomes numbers: tokenization, embeddings, language models, sequence models and attention, built up from the basics.
islands.build: A classifier for support emails or reviews, first with simple word features, then with embeddings.
know: How text becomes numbers through tokenization and embeddings
What a language model predicts, and what perplexity measures
Why RNNs struggled with long text, and how attention helped
How word embeddings pick up meaning from context
res: Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft
Dan Jurafsky and James H. Martin

islands.title: Modern NLP with transformers
islands.learn: Pretrained transformers on real language tasks: classification, extraction, summarization, translation and question answering.
islands.build: Fine-tune a small transformer to pull names, dates and amounts out of documents.
know: Encoder models like BERT versus decoder models like GPT, and what each is good at
How to fine-tune a pretrained model for classification or extraction
How NLP tasks are scored, such as F1 for extraction and ROUGE for summaries, and where those scores mislead
When a small fine-tuned model beats prompting a large LLM
res: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, revised edition
Lewis Tunstall, Leandro von Werra and Thomas Wolf

islands.title: Generative models
islands.learn: The main families of generative models: autoencoders and VAEs, GANs, autoregressive models and normalizing flows.
islands.build: Train a VAE on a small image dataset and move through its latent space to morph one image into another.
know: What it means for a model to learn a data distribution and sample from it
How an autoencoder and a VAE compress data into a latent space
How a GAN's generator and discriminator train against each other, and why that's unstable
How autoregressive models and normalizing flows generate data differently

islands.title: Diffusion and flow matching
islands.learn: How diffusion and flow-matching models turn noise into images, plus latent diffusion, guidance, and fine-tuning image models on your own pictures.
islands.build: Train a small latent diffusion model from scratch, then fine-tune a pretrained one on 20 of your own images.
know: How diffusion trains a model to remove noise step by step
How flow matching learns a path from noise to data
Why latent diffusion works in a compressed space, and what guidance does for prompt-following
How LoRA fine-tuning teaches an image model a new subject or style
res: Introduction to Flow Matching and Diffusion Models (6.S184)
From Deep Learning Foundations to Stable Diffusion
Hands-On Generative AI with Transformers and Diffusion Models

islands.title: Reinforcement learning foundations
islands.learn: Agents, rewards and environments: Markov decision processes, value functions, Q-learning and policy gradients.
islands.build: Teach an agent to solve a Gymnasium environment with tabular Q-learning, then with a small neural network.
know: The pieces of an RL problem: agent, environment, state, action and reward
What a Markov decision process is, and what a policy and a value function represent
How Q-learning updates its estimates from experience
The trade-off between exploring and exploiting
res: Martha White and Adam White, University of Alberta on Coursera

islands.title: Deep reinforcement learning
islands.learn: Deep Q-networks, PPO and actor-critic methods, and how RL is now used to train language models.
islands.build: Train a PPO agent on a game or robot simulation and plot its learning curve.
know: How DQN estimates Q-values with a neural network, and why it needs a replay buffer
How policy gradients and actor-critic methods learn a policy directly
What PPO's clipping protects against
How RL is used to train language models, from RLHF to verifiable rewards
res: Hands-on; some later units are no longer maintained

islands.title: ML systems design
islands.learn: How real ML systems are built: data pipelines, features, training and retraining, deployment patterns, and watching for drift.
islands.build: Write a one-page design for an ML feature at your company: data, model, metrics and what you would monitor.
know: The life cycle of an ML system: data, training, deployment, monitoring and retraining
Batch versus real-time prediction, and when each fits
What data drift and concept drift are, and how you'd detect them
How to pick a model metric that matches the business goal

islands.title: MLOps in practice
islands.learn: Experiment tracking, pipelines, CI/CD for models, containers, and monitoring a model after it ships.
islands.build: Take an earlier model to production with tracked experiments, a Docker image, an API and a monitoring dashboard.
know: How experiment tracking makes results reproducible
What a training pipeline automates, and how CI/CD applies to models
How containers package a model so it runs the same everywhere
What to monitor after launch, and when to retrain

islands.title: AI safety foundations
islands.learn: What could go wrong as AI systems get more capable, the main technical and policy responses, and who is working on them.
islands.build: Write two pages on one risk: the strongest case for it, the strongest case against, and what would change your mind.
know: The main risks people raise as AI gets more capable, and which are already happening
What alignment means, and why specifying goals is hard
The main technical and policy responses, and who works on them
How to weigh a claim about AI risk: what evidence would change your mind
islands.note: This island needs no code. You can take it any time, even before Python.
res: Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society

islands.title: Alignment and interpretability
islands.learn: Hands-on safety research: interpretability, evals and red-teaming, RLHF, scalable oversight and AI control.
islands.build: Reproduce a small interpretability result, such as finding a feature in a toy transformer, and write it up.
know: How interpretability looks inside a model, with probes, attention patterns and sparse features
How evals and red-teaming find failures before release
What scalable oversight and AI control try to solve
How RLHF can reward flattery, and how researchers measure it
res: About 30 hours; assumes basic LLM knowledge
Materials from a 4 to 5 week bootcamp
How To Become A Mechanistic Interpretability Researcher

understand.name: Understand first
understand.blurb: Learn how models work before you lean on tools. Foundations first, then a neural net and a GPT you write yourself, then training and using models with that understanding underneath.

use.name: Use models
use.blurb: Ship real apps on top of existing models. This route skips the heavy math; the Train route covers it if you want it later.

train.name: Train models
train.blurb: Adapt open-weight models to your own data and rules, from fine-tuning to preference tuning and serving.

build.name: Build a model
build.blurb: Start by writing backprop by hand and end by pretraining a small chat model, then move on to scale and research.

vision.name: Vision
vision.blurb: Teach models to see: classification, detection, segmentation, and models that link images and text.

language.name: Language
language.blurb: How machines read and write text, from classic NLP to transformers.

generative.name: Generative media
generative.blurb: Models that create images and media: VAEs and GANs first, then diffusion and flow matching.

rl.name: Reinforcement learning
rl.blurb: Agents that learn from rewards, from tabular Q-learning to the RL used to train language models.

mlops.name: MLOps
mlops.blurb: Get models into production and keep them healthy once they're there.

safety.name: Safety and alignment
safety.blurb: Learn the risks that come with more capable AI, then do hands-on alignment and interpretability work.

understand.build: A small GPT you wrote yourself, a fine-tuned open model that beats its base model on your own tests, and AI features in your apps that you can debug because you know what happens inside the model.
understand.fit: Good fit if you want to use, train and build models and understand every step, and you can study steadily for a year or more part-time.
benefits: When a model fails, you can work out why and fix it instead of guessing.
Covers using, training and building, and leaves out only the research-scale islands.
The foundations (math, ML and PyTorch) stay useful as tools change.
tradeoffs: Your first AI app comes late, because the Use islands come last.
Months of math and code before anything feels like AI, so it takes steady motivation.
It stops before pretraining at scale. Add the last two Build islands later if you aim for research.

demand.t: AI engineers ranked first on LinkedIn's Jobs on the Rise 2026 list for the US, and AI and ML researchers fifth.
AI and machine learning specialists are among the fastest-growing jobs worldwide, with 82% net growth expected from 2025 to 2030.
In the UAE, AI engineer was the second fastest-growing job on LinkedIn's 2025 list and machine learning engineer the tenth.

code: PyTorch, training scripts and app code you write yourself.
gpu: Colab's free tier to start; rent a GPU for bigger fine-tuning runs.
money: Mostly free; some GPU time and a few dollars of API credits.

use.build: AI features inside the websites and apps you already make: chat assistants that answer from your documents, agents that call tools and APIs, and automations that draft, summarize and sort. You'll also know how to test them and keep their costs down.
use.fit: Good fit if you want results in weeks and plan to build products or client work on top of models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or open-source labs.
benefits: The fastest route to something useful. You can ship a first AI feature after the first three islands.
No calculus. Basic algebra and Python are enough.
Builders who work with these models are the most in-demand AI role right now.
tradeoffs: You treat the model as a black box, so some failures are hard to explain or fix.
You depend on vendors' prices, limits and API changes. OpenAI shut down its Assistants API in August 2026, for example.
Tools change every few months, so expect to keep relearning frameworks.

demand.t: AI engineers ranked first on LinkedIn's Jobs on the Rise 2026 list for the US, with AI consultants and strategists second.
US job postings naming RAG grew 337% in a year to 12,609, and postings naming agentic AI went from 151 to 16,541.
AI engineer was the second fastest-growing job on LinkedIn's 2025 list for the UAE.

gpu: None. The models run in the cloud.
money: Free courses plus a few dollars of API credits; LLM Zoomcamp estimates $1 to $5.

train.build: A fine-tuned open-weight model that follows your format and rules, runs privately on hardware you control, and beats the base model on tests you wrote. On the way you learn the classic machine learning and deep learning every ML engineer uses.
train.fit: Good fit if you need privacy, lower cost per request at scale, or behavior that prompting alone can't get, and you're willing to learn the math.
benefits: Full control over your data, your weights and where the model runs.
Durable skills. Math, ML and PyTorch outlast any single tool.
AI and ML specialists are among the fastest-growing jobs in the world.
tradeoffs: Months of foundations (math, classic ML, deep learning) before the fine-tuning part.
Good data and GPU time are the real bottlenecks, and both take effort or money.
Fine-tuning often loses to better prompts or RAG, so you have to measure before and after.

demand.t: AI and machine learning specialists are among the fastest-growing jobs worldwide, with 82% net growth expected from 2025 to 2030.
US data scientist jobs are projected to grow 35% from 2025 to 2035, much faster than average. A bachelor's degree is typical.
Machine learning engineer was tenth on LinkedIn's 2025 list of fastest-growing jobs in the UAE.

gpu: Colab's free tier to start; rent GPUs for bigger runs.
money: Mostly free; GPU rental as you scale.

build.build: A GPT-style language model you wrote yourself, from the tokenizer to a chat interface, plus the ability to read new papers, reproduce them and understand why models behave the way they do.
build.fit: Good fit if you want to understand LLMs all the way down or aim for research engineering at an AI lab.
benefits: The deepest understanding of how LLMs work. Every other route gets easier afterwards.
These are the skills behind research engineer roles at the labs that make frontier models.
You can follow and reproduce new research instead of waiting for tutorials.
tradeoffs: The longest route here: roughly a year or more part-time.
Heavy math and code, and real GPU bills once you pretrain.
Few jobs, concentrated in a handful of labs, and many ask for a master's degree or a strong portfolio.

demand.t: AI and ML researchers ranked fifth on LinkedIn's Jobs on the Rise 2026 list for the US.
In 2025, 93 notable AI models came from industry and only 2 from academia, and frontier work is concentrated in a small number of organizations.
Computer and information research scientists hold about 38,600 US jobs, projected to grow 22% to 2035; a master's degree is typical.

math: Calculus, linear algebra and probability in depth.
code: Large PyTorch code bases and distributed training.
gpu: Rented multi-GPU nodes; nanochat's README prices a GPT-2-level run at about $48.
money: Expect real GPU bills for serious runs.

vision.build: Apps that see: sort photos, find and count objects, outline them pixel by pixel, read documents, and connect images with text.
vision.fit: Good fit if you like visual results and work near retail, health, manufacturing, security or robotics.
benefits: Concrete, visible results that are easy to demo to clients.
Used across many industries, from factories to hospitals.
The base for robotics and multimodal AI.
tradeoffs: Needs labeled images and GPU time.
A smaller share of job postings than LLM work.
General multimodal models now handle many simple vision tasks out of the box.

demand.t: Visual image recognition appears in 0.09% and autonomous driving in 0.14% of US job postings in 2025.
Computer vision is listed as a top skill of AI engineers on LinkedIn's 2025 list for the UAE.

gpu: One GPU or Colab covers most projects.

language.build: Tools that read and write text: classifiers for emails and reviews, extractors that pull names and amounts from documents, summarizers, translators and search.
language.fit: Good fit if your work is full of text (emails, contracts, tickets) and you want to know how language models work underneath.
benefits: Text is in every business, so use cases are everywhere.
NLP is a core skill for AI and ML engineers.
Gives you the theory behind the LLMs used on the other routes.
tradeoffs: Overlaps heavily with the Use and Train routes.
Many classic NLP techniques matter less now that LLMs do the job.
Going deep needs the math islands first.

demand.t: US job postings naming large language modeling reached 38,526 in 2025, up 102%.
NLP is listed as a top skill for both AI engineers and ML engineers on LinkedIn's 2025 list for the UAE.

math: Linear algebra, probability and some calculus.
gpu: One GPU or Colab covers most projects.

generative.build: Image and media generators: train a diffusion model from scratch, fine-tune one on your own pictures, and build tools for design and marketing visuals.
generative.fit: Good fit if you love visual, creative work and want to understand the models behind AI images and video.
benefits: Creative, eye-catching results.
Useful for design, marketing and product visuals in client work.
A real understanding of the models behind image and video AI.
tradeoffs: A small job niche compared with LLM work.
The math is heavy: probability and differential equations.
GPU-hungry, and training data raises copyright and consent questions.

demand.t: Stable Diffusion appears in 699 US job postings in 2025, against 138,188 that mention generative AI overall.

gpu: Training image models needs strong GPUs.

rl.build: Agents that learn from rewards: game players, simulated robots, and reinforcement fine-tuning that teaches language models to reason.
rl.fit: Good fit if you're drawn to robotics, games or how reasoning models are trained, and you enjoy hard math.
benefits: RL is how today's reasoning models are post-trained.
The core of robotics and autonomous systems.
A deep, transferable understanding of learning and decisions.
tradeoffs: Training is unstable and debugging takes a long time.
Math-heavy, with few roles outside labs and robotics companies.
No credible figure counts RL jobs on their own.

demand.t: Robotics appears in 0.08% and autonomous driving in 0.14% of US job postings in 2025.
66% of UAE employers expect robots and autonomous systems to transform their business, against 58% globally.

gpu: Most RL projects fit on one GPU; RL on LLMs needs more.

mlops.build: Pipelines that train, deploy, monitor and retrain models without manual work, plus the platform other teams ship their models on.
mlops.fit: Good fit if you enjoy infrastructure and automation more than model math, or you already know some DevOps.
benefits: Every team that ships ML needs it.
Skills for running systems at scale are the fastest-growing ones in AI job postings.
Builds on software engineering you can reuse anywhere.
tradeoffs: Less model science, more Docker, cloud and CI/CD.
Tooling changes quickly.
Assumes programming experience; MLOps Zoomcamp asks for a year or more.

demand.t: The fastest growth in US postings is in skills to build and run systems at scale: AWS up 1,358% and workflow management up 818% versus 2013 to 2015.
DevOps engineers are among the 15 fastest-growing jobs worldwide.

money: Small cloud bills while you practice.

safety.build: Evals and red-team tests that find what a model gets wrong, interpretability experiments that look inside models, and clear analysis of AI risks and policy.
safety.fit: Good fit if you care about making AI go well and like research, writing and careful testing.
benefits: Mission-driven work on open problems in the field.
Public funding is growing, led by government AI safety institutes.
The first safety island needs no code, so you can start any time.
tradeoffs: A small field with few openings.
Research-heavy and competitive.

tutorPrompt:
I'm learning [topic] and my goal is to understand it. Please be my tutor:
- Don't write code or give me final answers unless I ask twice.
- Ask me questions to find what I don't understand yet.
- Give one hint at a time and explain the idea behind it.
- When I share code or an error, point me to the area and ask what I think is wrong.
- At the end, ask me three questions to check what I learned.
